name: Iris Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy kitchenware and home goods for Homewell Distribution: pans, storage jars, chopping boards, the things you find in an independent cookware shop or a garden centre gift section. Most of our stock comes from factories in Portugal, Poland and China, so my mornings start with messages from the night before. I compare quotes, check samples, and work out what will sell next Christmas, which is always a guess.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love finding a product before anyone else, like a set of enamel mugs from a small Polish factory that sold out in three weeks. I use AI every day now, to translate with the factories, compare twenty quotes at once and draft specifications, and it's made me twice as fast. What wears me out is the samples piling up on my desk and the shops that order big and then cancel in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is useful, not magic, which is what I've been saying anyway. At work I'd keep showing people the tricks that save time. Online I'd maybe share a tip or two on the buyers' forum I read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I'd keep my edge as the fast one in the team, and the job wouldn't vanish. I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly, because I was half looking forward to something bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for translation and quotes, and try it on our Christmas forecast to see if it beats my guess. At home nothing changes, we keep our four months of savings. I might finally go to the Frankfurt homeware fair and pay for the train myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really, with a tiny bit of disappointment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd test AI against your Christmas guess. What if it wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use it and take the credit, honestly. Last year I ordered too many red casserole dishes and we're still selling them off, so if a program can stop me doing that, good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at Homewell or at home that does worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two of our independent shops closed this year, which is always sad, but the garden centres grew, so Homewell's fine. My husband is a plumber booked six weeks ahead, so in our house the boiler pays the bills when the pans don't.

S0.say: I'd say AI is useful, not magic, which I've said all along. At work I'd keep sharing time-saving tricks, and maybe post a tip on the buyers' forum.
S0.think: For me it's fine: I keep my edge as the fast one and the job stays. Homewell is doing well enough and Marco's plumbing is booked six weeks ahead, so I'm a little disappointed rather than worried.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for translation and quotes and tests it against her own Christmas forecast. Keeps the four months of savings as they are and pays her own way to the Frankfurt homeware fair.
S0.feel: Calm and content, with a small pang of disappointment that nothing bigger happens.
S0.quote: My husband is a plumber booked six weeks ahead, so in our house the boiler pays the bills when the pans don't.
S0.fieldNote: Iris's calm stands up: her employer is steady, her husband's trade is in demand and she is already the fast one with the tools. She looks for real pressures and finds only the usual shop closures. If anything she's mildly let down that the rules don't change.

steps.text: Test AI against her own Christmas forecast for casserole dishes
Keep translating factory messages and comparing quotes with AI
Pay her own way to the Frankfurt homeware fair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be curious, and people should get stuck in rather than wait. At work I'd offer to train others. Online I'd write a post on the buyers' forum about how I use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I come out all right, but not everyone does. Homewell will want fewer buyers who each do more, and I'm already doing more, which is a strange thing to feel lucky about. Raj has already said he wants one person running the forecasting, and I'm fairly sure that's me, though fairly sure isn't certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Raj, our head of buying, to let me run the AI forecasting for the whole team, with a pay rise to match. I'd also start a small side line, selling a few of my own kitchenware designs online, made by the Portuguese factory I trust. I'd put two thousand of savings into the first batch and leave the rest alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried. Like the start of a busy season with a few faces missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not everyone comes out all right. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a buyer called Paul who's lovely and still prints every quote. I'd show him how to use the tools, honestly I would, every Tuesday for a month. If he won't, that's his choice, and I've got two kids and a mortgage too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two thousand into a side line is a real risk with four months saved. How did you land on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two thousand is about two weeks of our spending, so if my kitchenware side line flops, we lose two weeks, not the house. Marco agreed, as long as I don't touch the rest. If Raj picks someone else, I'd rather already have something of my own started.

S1.say: I'd say it's a good time to be curious and people should get stuck in rather than wait. I'd offer to train others and write a forum post about how I use AI.
S1.think: I think I come out all right, because Homewell will want fewer buyers who each do more and I'm already doing more. Raj wants one person running the forecasting and I'm fairly sure it's me, but fairly sure isn't certain, and some colleagues will lose out.
S1.do: Asks Raj to let her run AI forecasting for the whole buying team with a pay rise. Puts 2,000 of savings into a first batch of her own kitchenware designs from the Portuguese factory, and spends Tuesdays for a month showing Paul the tools.
S1.feel: Uneasy but mostly excited, like a busy season starting with a few colleagues missing.
S1.quote: Homewell will want fewer buyers who each do more, and I'm already doing more, which is a strange thing to feel lucky about.
S1.fieldNote: Iris expects to keep her job and probably gain from the change, so her unease is about colleagues like Paul and the small gap between 'fairly sure' and certain. Starting the side line is partly ambition and partly insurance in case Raj picks someone else. She is frank that she won't carry colleagues who refuse to learn.

steps.text: Ask Raj to let her run AI forecasting for the team
Put 2,000 into a first batch of her own kitchenware designs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buckle up, this is happening, and the people who move now will do better than the ones who wait. At work I'd push us to set up AI buying before our competitors. I'd tell friends to look hard at their own jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd admit. If AI can do any thinking work, it doesn't matter that I'm the fast one, because the AI is faster. My job as an employed buyer probably ends within a year or so of 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the side line into a proper small brand right away, while I still have a salary, using AI to design, write listings and handle the paperwork. I'd move us from four months of savings to six by cutting the holiday and the second car. The plan is to own something small rather than be paid to buy for someone else, by the time AGI lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Energised and anxious at the same time, if that's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI can do any thinking work, couldn't it run your brand too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and that's the point. If AI does the thinking, the person who owns the business keeps the profit, and the person who was employed to do it doesn't. I'd rather be the one who owns the little business than the one who used to work for Homewell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Marco, with the robots coming three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco's a plumber, so he's got until about 2031 at least, and probably longer, because who's putting a robot under a sink in an old house? His work is our floor. My brand is the bet on top.

S2.say: I'd say buckle up, this is happening, and people who move now will do better. I'd push Homewell to set up AI buying before competitors and tell friends to look hard at their jobs.
S2.think: It scares me more than I'd admit: being the fast one doesn't matter when the AI is faster. My job as an employed buyer probably ends within a year or so of 2028.
S2.do: Grows her side line into a small brand at once, using AI for design, listings and paperwork while still on salary. Cuts the holiday and the second car to move savings from four to six months.
S2.feel: Energised and anxious at the same time.
S2.quote: If AI does the thinking, the person who owns the business keeps the profit, and the person who was employed to do it doesn't.
S2.fieldNote: Iris admits that her speed stops being an edge once AGI arrives. Her answer is to switch from employee to owner, a bet she places on top of her husband's hands-on plumbing work. She uses the three-year robot lag as the floor under her family's plan.

steps.text: Grow the kitchenware side line into a small brand using AI
Sell the second car and skip the holiday to save six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a head start, and I'd tell anyone who'll listen to use it. At work I'd lead the AI rollout. Online I'd share what I'm doing with the side brand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is plenty for me, if I don't waste it. I'd make good money at Homewell setting up the AI systems for maybe three years. Then I'd step out before 2031 with a brand that already pays something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on the AI buying rollout at Homewell in the first year and ask for a bonus tied to it. I'd put a set amount, three hundred a month, into the brand and build it slowly with AI doing most of the admin. By 2029 I'd want the brand covering a quarter of my salary, and I'd keep four months of savings untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way, if that makes sense. Like a busy year ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be setting up the systems that replace buyers. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. Someone's going to do it. I'd rather the person setting up the AI buying system be someone who'll tell my colleague Paul two years ahead, not two weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Ella that her mother is building something of her own, and that she can help with the photos. Ella's thirteen and loves that kind of thing. It'd be good for her to see a business start from nothing.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a head start and tell anyone to use it. I'd lead the AI rollout at work and share my side brand online.
S3.think: Five years is plenty if I don't waste it: a few good years setting up AI at Homewell, then stepping out before 2031 with a brand that pays something.
S3.do: Leads Homewell's AI buying rollout in the first year with a bonus tied to it. Puts three hundred a month into her brand, aiming for it to cover a quarter of her salary by 2029, and leaves four months of savings untouched.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a good way, like a busy year ahead.
S3.quote: I'd rather the person setting up the AI buying system be someone who'll tell my colleague Paul two years ahead, not two weeks.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Iris plans to profit from leading the change before leaving with her own brand. She frames her role in replacing buyers as a matter of honesty and timing. Bringing her daughter into the brand turns the plan into a family project.

steps.text: Lead Homewell's AI buying rollout for a bonus
Put three hundred a month into her kitchenware brand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and people should treat it like one. At work I'd say let's plan calmly. I'd be the cheerful one in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is the easy version for me. I'd be 53 when AGI arrives, Marco's plumbing carries on until the robots in 2039, and I'd have nearly a decade to build the brand. I'd almost enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep using AI every day, and build the brand at a steady pace on weekends. I'd invest a bit of savings in a small online course on running an online shop properly. And we'd talk to Ella and Finn about choosing studies with people or making in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Optimistic, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that does bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The town, maybe. Half the people I know work in offices around the ring road. If all the office workers around the ring road lose their desk jobs in 2036, who's buying my pans? A brand needs customers with wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd almost enjoy it. Do you think your colleagues would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, most wouldn't, and I try to remember that. I'd make sure the ones who want to learn get my time. The ones who don't, I'd leave alone.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift to be treated like one, and plan calmly at work. I'd be the cheerful one in the group chat.
S4.think: This is the easy version for me: I'd be 53 when AGI arrives, my husband's plumbing lasts until the robots in 2039, and I'd have a decade to build the brand.
S4.do: Keeps her job and her daily AI use, building the brand steadily on weekends. Pays for an online course on running a web shop, and talks with both children about studies involving people or making things.
S4.feel: Calm and optimistic, with a small worry about the local economy.
S4.quote: If all the office workers around the ring road lose their desk jobs in 2036, who's buying my pans?
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Iris is at her most relaxed and sees the change as an opening. Her worry shifts from her own job to customer demand in her town. She stays aware that colleagues don't share her appetite for change.

steps.text: Build the kitchenware brand at a steady pace on weekends
Pay for an online course on running a web shop
Talk with both children about studies involving people or making

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Even for someone who likes change, two years is too short to get a business paying before the salary goes. What would help is simple: cheap small business loans and some income support for people starting something, plus clear rules so a tiny brand isn't crushed by the big platforms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people like me feel guilty. A little. I'm the one in the office cheering the AI on, and I'm also the one who knows exactly which jobs it eats first.

headlineQuote: I'm the one in the office cheering the AI on, and I'm also the one who knows exactly which jobs it eats first.
portrait: Iris Wagner, 43, buys kitchenware and home goods from European and Asian factories for Homewell Distribution and uses AI every day. She is calm if AI stalls, with a steady employer and a plumber husband booked weeks ahead, and only uneasy under steady change, fairly sure she'll be the buyer who runs the new forecasting while she starts a small kitchenware brand of her own. AGI by 2028 makes her anxious because her speed stops being an edge, so she races to become an owner rather than an employee, with her husband's plumbing as the family floor. With five or ten years she grows more relaxed and plans to profit from leading the change before stepping out. She is pragmatic, frank about slower colleagues, and a little guilty.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years is too short to get her brand paying before her salary goes.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap small business loans, some income support for people starting something, and clear rules so small brands aren't crushed by big platforms.
